--- title: "09 — Joint MIMO modal identification" description: "A coupled 6-DoF suspension under closed-loop damping, identified jointly through the live loops: one Pintelon–Schoukens multisine per actuator recovers the open-loop coupled FRF, and a rank-1 modal fit (shared poles, per-mode rank-1 mode shapes) returns every modal frequency and Q with a Cramér–Rao envelope. The init is data-driven, so it needs no accurate prior." image: thumbnails/09.svg categories: [MIMO, closed-loop, modal] freeze: true --- The earlier MIMO example identifies a 2×2 plant element by element. This one fits the whole coupled plant **jointly**: a six-degree-of-freedom suspension running in a closed damping loop, where every transfer-function element shares the same modal poles. The measurement is the same Pintelon–Schoukens recipe — one periodic multisine per actuator, a leakage-free reference FRF, a per-bin noise model — and the new piece is a parametric step on top of it that ties all the elements to a common set of modes. ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## A six-mode demonstration The twin is a coupled normal-mode plant with six shared modes (representative low-frequency suspension values), driven through six diagonal velocity dampers. It is a *demonstration* of the joint-fit measurement, not a validated suspension model, and six modes are not a proof that the method scales without limit. The page is rendered with `freeze: true`. ::: ::: {#138a1cf3 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Setup — import the presentation glue"} import sys, pathlib _p = pathlib.Path.cwd() for _c in [_p, *_p.parents]: if (_c / "docs" / "rank1_modal_demo.py").exists() and str(_c / "docs") not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c / "docs")) if (_c / "rank1_modal_demo.py").exists() and str(_c) not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c)) import numpy as np import rank1_modal_demo as rm ``` ::: ## The plant and the loop The coupled plant `G(s)` has six shared modal poles; coupling lives in the mode shapes, so the diagonal elements carry anti-resonance notches and the off-diagonal elements carry notch-free cross terms. It runs closed: six diagonal velocity dampers act through the input and output decoupling matrices, so the suspension never sits open while it is measured. The campaign drives each actuator in turn with a band-limited multisine and reads all drive monitors and sensors through the live loops. ## Step 1 — the open-loop coupled FRF Because the twin simulates consistently (`u_drive = S·u_exc`, then `y_sens = G·u_drive`), the per-bin matrix recovery `G = Y·X⁻¹` returns the **open-loop** coupled FRF even though the data were taken closed. That inverse is exact off-resonance but noisy near the resonances, where the drive monitors are small. ## Step 2 — the rank-1 modal fit The parametric model shares one set of modal poles `(a_k, b_k)` across all elements and gives each mode a rank-1 residue `R_k = φ_k ψ_kᵀ` — a sensor mode shape `φ_k` times an actuator mode shape `ψ_k`. The fit is a sample-ML (IQML) minimization on the raw spectra with a per-bin weighting, and its Cramér–Rao bound propagates to both a per-bin FRF envelope and a per-mode `(f0, Q)` uncertainty. The figure below shows one diagonal element `G[0,0]` and one off-diagonal `G[0,3]`: the nonparametric `|Gnp|` (markers, noisy near the peaks), the rank-1 `|Gfit|` with its ±1σ band, and the analytic truth. The parametric fit predicts cleanly **through** the resonances where the per-bin inverse scatters. ::: {#5aad60e4 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Through-resonance recovery — G[0,0] and G[0,3]"} rm.through_resonance_fig() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Modal recovery All six modal frequencies come back through the loops to ~0.15 %, and the deviations sit inside the Cramér–Rao bars — the recovered `(fit − truth)` residual and its ±1σ envelope: ::: {#93558deb .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Modal frequency residual ± CRB, per mode"} rm.modal_recovery_fig() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {#54122dd4 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Recovered modes — truth vs fit ± σ"} from IPython.display import display display(rm.modal_table()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **Joint-MIMO modal recovery through the live loops** | mode | truth f₀ [Hz] | fitted f₀ ± σ [Hz] | fitted Q ± σ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | mode 1 | 0.450 | 0.4496 ± 0.0002 | 19.6 ± 0.1 | | mode 2 | 0.600 | 0.5997 ± 0.0002 | 25.5 ± 0.2 | | mode 3 | 0.800 | 0.7996 ± 0.0001 | 18.2 ± 0.1 | | mode 4 | 1.000 | 0.9997 ± 0.0001 | 30.3 ± 0.2 | | mode 5 | 1.500 | 1.4993 ± 0.0001 | 35.0 ± 0.2 | | mode 6 | 2.200 | 2.1979 ± 0.0004 | 28.1 ± 0.2 | ::: ::: ## The init is data-driven The fit is started from a peak-pick on the recovered FRF: the summed power `Σᵢⱼ|Gnp(f)|²` is searched for its six strongest peaks, and those seed the pole frequencies. No accurate prior is used — the modes are found from the data — which is why the recovery is the same whether the design model was right or badly wrong. ::: {#054d3863 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Peak-pick on the recovered FRF power"} rm.peak_pick_fig() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## What this shows, and what it does not On this twin the joint fit recovers all six modal frequencies to ~0.15 % through the live damping loops, with Q to a few percent and a Cramér–Rao envelope consistent with the deviations. It is a six-mode demonstration of the rank-1 modal step on a representative coupled plant — not a validated suspension model, and not a claim that the method scales without limit. The honest next test is a higher-order, measured plant under a real decoupling design.
